builder_plan.scenario: A workflow needs specialist review, but extra agents may add more cost than useful work.
builder_plan.change: Test the proposed division of work against a single-agent implementation.
builder_plan.baseline: One agent with the same tools and an equal total token and time budget.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Accepted outputs, coordination failures, wall-clock time, and total cost across all agents.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Who Should Know What? Empirical Information Design for Multi-Agent LLM Economies
summary: The framework replaces the default of giving every agent full or arbitrary context by systematically testing which information-sharing policy (ordinal vs. exact valuations, partial vs. full disclosure) each deployed model handles best, holding interaction rules fixed. It costs repeated simulation runs of the multi-agent market across candidate policies and models, plus engineering effort to implement configurable observation layers in the agent harness. It can fail because results are strongly model-dependent, so a policy tuned for one model may degrade outcomes after a model upgrade, and simulated market behavior may not transfer to the production task distribution.
rationale: Any team running multi-agent LLM workflows via APIs can adopt configurable disclosure cheaply, but the paper shows gains are model-specific and can reverse sign, so per-deployment validation is mandatory before committing.
technique: Empirical information design for multi-agent disclosure policies

claims.statement: The framework replaces the default of giving every agent full or arbitrary context by systematically testing which information-sharing policy (ordinal vs. exact valuations, partial vs. full disclosure) each deployed model handles best, holding interaction rules fixed. It costs repeated simulation runs of the multi-agent market across candidate policies and models, plus engineering effort to implement configurable observation layers in the agent harness. It can fail because results are strongly model-dependent, so a policy tuned for one model may degrade outcomes after a model upgrade, and simulated market behavior may not transfer to the production task distribution.

Disclosure granularity moves realized welfare by large, model-dependent margins: e.g., trade gains shift from 98% to 91% of maximum for one model (worse with exact valuations) and 72% to 86% for another (better); in double auctions full disclosure lowers welfare from 97% to 78%, 94% to 64%, and 97% to 62% for three frontier models.
